structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment due to unequal life advantages, a principle that made him a confidant to college peers but left him disillusioned after returning from the East last autumn, except for Gatsby, whom he views as uniquely hopeful and gifted with romantic sensitivity. In the spring of 1922, Nick rents a modest eighty-dollar bungalow in West Egg, overlooking Long Island Sound between two grand estates, one belonging to the mysterious Jay Gatsby; after feeling isolated, he gains a sense of belonging when a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village, and he purchases twelve volumes on banking as symbols of his ambition to become a 'well-rounded man.' He drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a domineering Yale acquaintance, at their opulent Georgian Colonial home, where he meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker. During an evening dinner marked by tension, Tom aggressively promotes racist theories from 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' a phone call interrupts the meal prompting Daisy to fabricate a story about the butler’s nose, and she later reveals her despair by declaring she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool,' while Jordan confides in Nick that Tom has a mistress in New York. Later, alone in the crimson room as Jordan reads from the Saturday Evening Post and departs, Daisy and Tom press Nick about engagement rumors from the West, which he denies, and Tom warns him not to believe everything he hears; as Nick drives home to West Egg under a bright summer night, he sees Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, stretching his arms toward a distant green light at the end of a dock, trembling before vanishing into the darkness.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to New York, stopping at the desolate Valley of Ashes where Tom forces Nick to meet his mistress, Myrtle Wilson, at her husband George Wilson’s run-down garage beneath the looming eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg. Myrtle and Tom board separate train cars to avoid social exposure; en route, Myrtle purchases a moving-picture magazine, Town Tattle, cold cream, perfume, and impulsively buys a dog from a street vendor, insisting it is male despite Tom’s correction. They arrive at a top-floor apartment on 158th Street, cluttered with oversized tapestried furniture and an enlarged photograph of Myrtle’s mother, where Myrtle calls her sister Catherine and the McKees to join them. Tom pours whisky, and Nick becomes drunk for the second time in his life; Myrtle changes into a cream-coloured chiffon dress and adopts an exaggerated, haughty persona. As the party escalates, Catherine falsely claims Daisy Buchanan is a Catholic who refuses divorce, prompting Myrtle to defiantly shout Daisy’s name—triggering Tom to violently break her nose with his open hand. The apartment descends into chaos as women rush to tend to Myrtle, Chester McKee awakens dazed and leaves, and Nick escapes with him by elevator, later finding himself alone in a cold Pennsylvania Station at dawn.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The drunken man in the library
structure.summary: On a Saturday evening in West Egg, Nick Carraway arrives at Jay Gatsby’s mansion by car to attend an extravagant party filled with guests arriving via Rolls-Royce and station wagons, where orchestral music, imported champagne, and lavish food create an atmosphere of excess. Amid gossip about Gatsby’s mysterious past—including rumors he killed a man or was a German spy—Nick reconnects with Jordan Baker and encounters a drunken man in the library who marvels at the authenticity of Gatsby’s real books, then speaks with a war veteran who offers him a hydroplane ride without revealing his name. After wandering through the chaotic party, Nick is shocked to discover that the man he had been chatting with over champagne is Gatsby himself, whose rare smile and polished demeanor contrast with the wild behavior of guests, including a chorus girl weeping with ink-stained tears, marital fights erupting, and wives being carried out kicking; Gatsby invites Nick to ride his hydroplane the next morning, then summons Jordan alone, leaving her visibly shaken with an unspoken revelation. As the party ends, a new coupe crashes into a ditch outside, and Owl Eyes insists he wasn’t driving, revealing another sober, confused man who asks for the nearest gas station, while Gatsby stands alone on the porch bidding farewell with formal grace as Nick departs under a faint moon.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, church bells ring as a chaotic parade of guests arrives by car from East Egg, West Egg, and New York to Gatsby’s mansion, where Nick Carraway observes a transient crowd of aristocrats, bootleggers, and scandalous socialites—many named in a crumbling 1922 timetable—who spread rumors about Gatsby’s origins while engaging in excess that ends in tragedy, such as Snell’s crushed hand and Palmetto’s suicide. Later that day, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-note horn, inviting him to lunch; during the drive to New York, Gatsby presents an elaborate but implausible personal history—including Oxford, wartime honors, and European aristocracy—backed by a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph, while revealing he wishes to make a request involving Jordan Baker. At noon in a cellar on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a man with ivory cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts Rosy Rosenthal’s murder and reveals Gatsby fixed the 1919 World Series; Gatsby abruptly leaves and vanishes after Nick Carraway introduces him to Tom Buchanan. In a flashback to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls meeting Daisy Fay in Louisville with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby, who later married Tom Buchanan after a dramatic wedding-day episode involving a drunk refusal to release a three-hundred-fifty-thousand-dollar pearl necklace; six weeks prior to the present, Jordan mentions Gatsby’s name to Nick, prompting Daisy to realize he is the same officer from 1917. After leaving the Plaza, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he now asks Nick Carraway to invite Daisy to tea so he can visit her unseen, fearing to ask Jordan directly and insisting Daisy remain unaware of the arrangement.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a late night in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but silent, with Gatsby nervously asking him to arrange a tea with Daisy and awkwardly probing his finances before offering a vague business opportunity, which Nick declines. The next morning, heavy rain falls as Gatsby sends a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers; he arrives in a white flannel suit, silver shirt, and gold tie, visibly shaken. When Daisy arrives by car, Gatsby trembles upon entering the house, nearly knocking over a mantel clock, and the meeting begins in stifling silence before dissolving into quiet intimacy, leaving Daisy tear-stained and Gatsby radiant. After the rain stops, Gatsby enthusiastically invites Daisy to tour his mansion, where they pass through opulent, eerily empty rooms—Marie Antoinette music-rooms, Restoration Salons, and period bedrooms—until they discover Mr. Klipspringer doing exercises in pajamas. In Gatsby’s study, he throws a cascade of exquisite shirts onto the table, overwhelming Daisy into sobs as she admires their beauty. Later, as rain resumes, Gatsby points to the green light at Daisy’s dock, acknowledging its diminished symbolism now that she is present; Nick examines photographs of Mr. Dan Cody and a youthful Gatsby in yachting attire, while Daisy nostalgically admires his old pompadour. When Klipspringer is summoned to play piano, his awkward performance of songs like 'The Love Nest' is interrupted as Gatsby and Daisy reconnect emotionally, leaving Nick as an outsider who departs alone into the rain, observing Gatsby’s uncertain happiness and Daisy’s full absorption in him.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a New York reporter arriving at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement amid rumors of his involvement in underground activities, including the absurd claim that he lives in a moving boat resembling a house; the narrative then shifts to Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who at seventeen rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht, the Tuolomee, anchored off Lake Superior, and spent five years serving in multiple roles aboard—steward, mate, skipper, secretary, and jailor—before being cheated out of his $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye after Cody’s death, yet retaining the refined persona and habits that transformed him into Jay Gatsby. Later, after weeks of absence, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists on serving drinks and inviting them to supper, but their cold detachment and Sloane’s subtle dismissal prompt them to leave abruptly, leaving Gatsby standing alone. Days later, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is overwhelmed by the vulgarity and chaos of West Egg’s atmosphere, and afterward, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway that she did not enjoy the evening and insists he can repeat the past—specifically, he wants Daisy to declare she never loved Tom so they can return to Louisville and rekindle their five-year-old romance, recalling a moonlit night when he first kissed her as a moment of transcendent revelation.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ estate to find Gatsby waiting; Gatsby has replaced all former servants with silent newcomers to conceal Daisy’s secret afternoon visits. During a stifling luncheon, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, shocking Tom, who becomes suspicious as Gatsby is stunned by the presence of their daughter Pammy, whom he had not believed existed. After a heated exchange over Gatsby’s Oxford claim and criminal ties to Meyer Wolfsheim, the group departs for town in two cars: Tom, Nick, and Jordan in Gatsby’s car, while Daisy and Gatsby follow in Tom’s coupé. They stop at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where a sick and distraught Wilson reveals his plan to take Myrtle away, while Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife. The group then arrives at the Plaza Hotel, where Tom aggressively exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging past and forces Daisy to choose between them; she admits she once loved Tom but also loved Gatsby, yet ultimately refuses to renounce Tom entirely. Tom orders them back to Long Island in Gatsby’s car, effectively ending the confrontation. That evening, Myrtle Wilson is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car while running into the road after screaming from upstairs; Michaelis witnesses the aftermath, and Tom and Nick arrive to find Wilson hysterical over her body. Tom denies owning the yellow car, claiming his own is blue, and is visibly shaken. Later, Nick waits outside the Buchanan house alone, where Gatsby confesses Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle and insists he will take the blame to protect her. Nick observes Tom and Daisy quietly sharing food in the kitchen, confirming their enduring bond, as Gatsby refuses to leave, choosing instead to wait all night outside Daisy’s window.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window—she briefly appeared, then turned off the light. The two search the neglected, dusty mansion for cigarettes and smoke by the open French windows, where Gatsby, refusing to leave, recounts his youth with Dan Cody and his first love for Daisy, confessing he courted her under false pretenses of wealth and became irrevocably bound to her as if married. On the last afternoon before his departure abroad, Gatsby and Daisy share a silent, tender intimacy in his room by a fire, their gestures sealing a profound emotional connection that overshadowed all his ambitions. Meanwhile, Daisy, trapped in a world of orchids and all-night parties, grows emotionally fragile and chooses Tom Buchanan after his arrival offers her decisive stability; the letter informing Gatsby of her decision reaches him while he is mistakenly sent to Oxford. Later, Gatsby recalls returning penniless to Louisville after their wedding, walking the streets haunted by memories, and reaching desperately for a fading image of Daisy as the train pulled away—realizing he lost the 'freshest and best' part of that time. On the same day, Gatsby refuses to drain the pool, revealing he never used it all summer; Nick Carraway, missing two trains, shouts that Gatsby is worth more than Tom and Daisy’s 'rotten crowd,' to which Gatsby responds with a radiant smile recalling his solitary figure on the steps. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief after Myrtle’s death, fixates on the yellow car and the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, declaring 'God sees everything.' He travels on foot to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, then to West Egg, where he learns Gatsby’s name. At two o’clock, Gatsby puts on his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, instructs the butler to bring calls to him at the pool, and insists the open car remain untouched despite its damaged fender. He walks alone toward the pool; no call comes. At four o’clock, gunshots are heard by the chauffeur, who dismisses them. Nick Carraway arrives from the station, raises the alarm, and together with the butler, chauffeur, and gardener, they find Gatsby’s body floating on the mattress in the pool; only then does the gardener discover Wilson’s body in the grass.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left alone to manage the chaotic influx of police, photographers, and reporters at Gatsby’s mansion, where children sneak in through the yard; official reports label Wilson a 'madman' and Catherine falsely testifies under oath to sever any link between Myrtle and Gatsby. Nick Carraway desperately tries to reach Daisy, Meyer Wolfsheim, and others by phone and letter, receiving only silence—until a mistaken long-distance call from Chicago assumes Gatsby is alive, prompting Nick Carraway to bluntly announce, 'Mr. Gatsby’s dead.' On the third day, Henry C. Gatz, Gatsby’s father, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly shaken and unable to eat, and is shown Gatsby’s body and the mansion, where he reveals a photograph of the house and an old notebook detailing Gatsby’s boyhood self-improvement schedule; nearly all acquaintances refuse to attend the funeral, including Klipspringer, who asks for tennis shoes, and Wolfsheim, who cites a personal rule against involvement after death. The funeral at Gatsby’s house is attended only by Gatz, the Lutheran minister from Flushing, and Nick Carraway, as rain falls. Later, in a thick drizzle at five o’clock, a procession of three cars—motor hearse, limousine carrying Gatz and the minister, and Gatsby’s station wagon with servants and the postman—arrives at the cemetery, where the owl-eyed man, whom Nick Carraway does not know by name, appears unexpectedly, wipes his rain-soaked glasses to view the canvas-shrouded grave, murmurs 'Amen to that' after someone says 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' and sadly concludes, 'The poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick Carraway reflects on his Midwestern roots through memories of Chicago’s Union Station in December, the sight of yellow railroad cars, and winter nights with snow twinkling against windows, defining his identity not by geography but by emotional recollections; he realizes he, Gatsby, Daisy, Tom, and Jordan were all Westerners who failed to adapt to the East, which he now sees as a nightmarish distortion like an El Greco painting. He meets Jordan Baker, learns she is engaged to another man, and endures her accusation that he is dishonest, to which he replies he is too old to deceive himself about honor. On a late October afternoon, he encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as truth for a man who was 'armed and threatening,' while emotionally recounting grief over dog biscuits left at his flat; Nick Carraway sees Tom and Daisy as careless people who destroy lives and retreat into wealth. He shakes Tom’s hand with pity as Tom enters a jewelry store to buy a pearl necklace or cuff buttons, finally freeing him from moral unease. In a final visit to the abandoned mansion at night, Nick Carraway finds an obscene word scrawled on the white steps, erases it with his shoe, walks to the beach, and contemplates the vanished natural beauty of the island once seen by Dutch sailors, drawing a parallel between that lost wonder and Gatsby’s futile pursuit of Daisy and the green light, concluding with the metaphor of humanity striving against the current, forever pulled back into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
Nick Carraway, a Midwesterner disillusioned by the East, moves to West Egg in the spring of 1922 and rents a modest home beside the lavish mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, arrogant residents of East Egg—Nick is introduced to the glittering yet hollow world of Jazz Age excess. He also meets the cynical, independent Jordan Baker, who reveals Tom’s affair with Myrtle Wilson, a woman trapped in the desolate Valley of Ashes. As Nick becomes increasingly drawn into Gatsby’s orbit, he learns that Gatsby’s opulent parties and mysterious persona are all orchestrated to win back Daisy, the woman he loved five years earlier before the war. Gatsby’s wealth, built through bootlegging and criminal ties under the mentorship of Meyer Wolfsheim, is a performance designed to make him worthy of Daisy, whose voice he once described as full of money.

The rising action centers on Gatsby’s desperate attempt to rekindle his romance with Daisy, facilitated by Nick’s reluctant mediation. After a tense, emotional reunion at Nick’s cottage, Gatsby and Daisy are briefly reconnected, but their fragile rekindling is shattered when Tom Buchanan confronts Gatsby at the Plaza Hotel. There, Gatsby’s fabricated past collapses under scrutiny, and Daisy, overwhelmed and uncertain, admits she once loved both men but ultimately cannot abandon the security Tom provides. The confrontation ends with Tom forcing them to return to Long Island in Gatsby’s car, while Myrtle Wilson, mistaking the vehicle for Tom’s, runs into the road and is killed. Though Daisy was driving, Gatsby resolves to take the blame, shielding her from consequence. Meanwhile, Myrtle’s husband George Wilson, misled by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer, descends into grief-fueled madness, fixating on the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg as divine judgment.

The climax arrives with Gatsby’s murder: Wilson tracks him to his mansion and shoots him in the pool before taking his own life. Nick is left alone to arrange Gatsby’s funeral, only to find that the society Gatsby cultivated has vanished—no guests attend, no calls are returned, not even Meyer Wolfsheim or Jordan Baker. Gatsby’s father arrives from Minnesota, revealing the boyhood dreams and self-improvement logs that shaped the man Gatsby became, underscoring the tragic gap between aspiration and reality. Nick, disillusioned by the East’s moral decay, reflects on the American Dream’s corruption, comparing Gatsby’s futile pursuit of Daisy to the original Dutch sailors’ awe at an unspoiled New World. He realizes Gatsby’s dream was not merely for a woman but for a perfect, unreachable past, and as he stands on the beach one last time, he sees the green light across the bay as a symbol of all human striving—eternally receding, forever pulled back into the past. Nick departs for the Midwest, having survived the chaos with his moral compass intact, though deeply scarred.
